items.text: Characteristics & Challenges of UbiComp To understand how Ubiquitous Computing (UbiComp) differs from a standard desktop computer, we must look at its core characteristics and the unique problems it creates for developers.

items.title: Core Characteristics of UbiComp
items.snippet: Invisibility (Calm Computing) The technology fades into the background. Users do not need to actively stare at a screen or type on a…
items.text: Invisibility (Calm Computing) The technology fades into the background. Users do not need to actively stare at a screen or type on a keyboard; the environment itself is the interface, operating quietly without demanding constant attention. Context-Awareness The system constantly gathers data about its surroundings. It knows the time of day, the temperature, your physical location, and even your current activity, allowing it to anticipate what you need before you ask. Interconnectedness Devices do not operate alone. Multiple devices (wearables, smart appliances, room sensors) are constantly communicating and sharing data with each other over a network to create a seamless experience.

items.title: The Challenges of UbiComp
items.snippet: Privacy and Security UbiComp environments constantly monitor users (using cameras, microphones, and location trackers), creating a massive…
items.text: Privacy and Security UbiComp environments constantly monitor users (using cameras, microphones, and location trackers), creating a massive risk of data breaches, unauthorized surveillance, and the unethical selling of personal habits to third parties. Maintaining the Hardware Layer UbiComp systems rely entirely on a robust, physical hardware layer consisting of thousands of embedded sensors, microcontrollers, and wireless transmitters. If this hardware layer loses power, breaks, or disconnects from the internet, the entire "smart" environment completely stops working. items.text: Introduction & Review of HCI Fundamentals Computer Science, which develops software applications Psychology, which studies how users process information Design, which organizes layout, typography, and color Ergonomics, which considers physical comfort and strain

items.title: What does Ergonomics (Human Factors) ensure in technology design?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 1: Introduction & Review of HCI Fundamentals
items.text: Introduction & Review of HCI Fundamentals Software architecture supports the application's functions. Hardware is comfortable and does not cause physical strain. Visual layouts communicate information clearly to users. Cognitive demands do not overload the user's attention.

items.title: What is the core goal of HCI 1?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 1: Introduction & Review of HCI Fundamentals
items.text: Introduction & Review of HCI Fundamentals Usability, including ease of learning and user satisfaction Immersive technology, including virtual and augmented reality Conversational AI, including chatbots and voice interfaces Smart environments, including connected physical devices

items.title: What is the design philosophy where the needs and limitations of the end-user are the focus at every stage?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 1: Introduction & Review of HCI Fundamentals
items.text: Introduction & Review of HCI Fundamentals Traditional problem-solving focused on predefined goals System-centered development focused on technical convenience User-Centered Design focused on people's needs and limitations Backend development focused on software architecture

items.title: What is Don Norman’s Gulf of Execution?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 1: Introduction & Review of HCI Fundamentals
items.text: Introduction & Review of HCI Fundamentals The gap between system feedback and user understanding The gap between a user's goal and available system actions The difference between low- and high-fidelity prototypes The difference between user research and usability testing

items.title: Why is integrating HCI important in systems development?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 1: Introduction & Review of HCI Fundamentals
items.text: Introduction & Review of HCI Fundamentals It prioritizes backend code even when interfaces are confusing. It reduces user errors, training time, and support costs. It replaces the need to understand users and their problems. It requires users to adapt to the system's existing design.

items.title: What does HCI 2 focus on compared to HCI 1?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 1: Introduction & Review of HCI Fundamentals
items.text: Introduction & Review of HCI Fundamentals Basic desktop and mobile buttons, menus, and layouts Standard screen navigation and traditional interface controls Emotion, immersive technologies, smart environments, and AI Programming languages, application code, and software architecture

items.title: Which technology involves the physical room itself becoming the computer?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 1: Introduction & Review of HCI Fundamentals
items.text: Introduction & Review of HCI Fundamentals Virtual Reality, which immerses users in digital environments Augmented Reality, which overlays graphics onto the real world Ubiquitous Computing, which embeds computing into everyday spaces Conversational AI, which supports spoken or written interaction

items.title: What is Design Thinking?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 2: Design Thinking & UCD Process
items.text: Design Thinking & UCD Process A linear process that follows a predefined technical plan An iterative process for understanding users and redefining problems A method focused mainly on completing software code A strategy that begins with technology and finds buyers

items.title: What is the foundation principle of Design Thinking?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 2: Design Thinking & UCD Process
items.text: Design Thinking & UCD Process Technical convenience when developing software Empathy for users' experiences, feelings, and frustrations Fast implementation of a predefined business goal Final testing after the product has been completed

items.title: How does iteration work in Design Thinking?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 2: Design Thinking & UCD Process
items.text: Design Thinking & UCD Process Teams follow one fixed path from planning to release. Teams create, test, learn, and refine their solutions. Teams avoid failure by skipping early prototypes. Teams wait until launch before gathering user feedback.

items.title: How does traditional problem-solving differ from Design Thinking?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 2: Design Thinking & UCD Process
items.text: Design Thinking & UCD Process Traditional problem-solving always begins with user empathy. Traditional problem-solving often assumes the initial problem is correct. Traditional problem-solving depends on continuous prototyping. Traditional problem-solving regularly redefines the original problem.

items.title: What is the critical first stage in the Four UCD Process Stages?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 2: Design Thinking & UCD Process
items.text: Design Thinking & UCD Process Evaluating the prototype against user requirements Identifying users, goals, devices, and the context of use Designing low- and high-fidelity interface prototypes Combining business goals with user requirements

items.title: What does the 'Specify user requirements' stage do?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 2: Design Thinking & UCD Process
items.text: Design Thinking & UCD Process It combines user and business goals into clear requirements. It tests whether the final interface satisfies its users. It develops wireframes and interactive interface prototypes. It identifies the devices and environment used by people.

items.title: When should Design Thinking primarily be applied?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 2: Design Thinking & UCD Process
items.text: Design Thinking & UCD Process During final usability testing of the interface After software development and product release During early product strategy and problem discovery During backend implementation after requirements are fixed

items.title: What is an empathy map used for?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 2: Design Thinking & UCD Process
items.text: Design Thinking & UCD Process To organize software architecture and technical components To describe what users say, think, do, and feel To measure the numerical results of user surveys To outline the screen structure of a digital prototype

items.title: What are personas?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 2: Design Thinking & UCD Process
items.text: Design Thinking & UCD Process Data-driven fictional profiles representing different user types Visual diagrams showing users' emotional highs and lows Rough sketches showing early interface layouts Interview transcripts containing users' spoken responses

items.title: What visual storyline identifies user pain points by tracking emotional highs and lows over time?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 2: Design Thinking & UCD Process
items.text: Design Thinking & UCD Process An empathy map describing what users think and feel A journey map tracking actions, interactions, and emotions A wireframe outlining the structure of an interface A persona representing a particular group of users

items.title: What is a mental model built from?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 3: Cognitive Models & Mental Models
items.text: Cognitive Models & Mental Models Objective instructions provided in a system manual Past experiences and expectations about how systems work Technical rules written in the application's source code Design decisions made by the system's developer

items.title: What happens when a system behaves differently than a user's mental model?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 3: Cognitive Models & Mental Models
items.text: Cognitive Models & Mental Models Users immediately understand the unexpected interaction. The mismatch can cause confusion, errors, and task failure. The interface automatically becomes easier to operate. Users no longer need feedback from the system.

items.title: What principle refers to physical or visual clues that tell a user how an object can be interacted with?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 3: Cognitive Models & Mental Models
items.text: Cognitive Models & Mental Models Affordance, which suggests possible ways to interact Visibility, which makes important functions easy to find Feedback, which shows the result of a user's action Iteration, which improves a design through repeated testing

items.title: What is the system's immediate response to a user's action called?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 3: Cognitive Models & Mental Models
items.text: Cognitive Models & Mental Models Visibility, which makes important controls easy to locate Feedback, which communicates the result of an action Affordance, which suggests how an object can be used Mental model, which represents a user's expectations

items.title: What are the two main phases of Norman’s Model of Interaction?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 3: Cognitive Models & Mental Models
items.text: Cognitive Models & Mental Models Planning and coding, which prepare and build a system Execution and evaluation, which involve acting and checking results Empathy and iteration, which guide user-centered design Input and output, which describe information entering and leaving

items.title: In the GOMS model, what do the 'Operators' represent?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 3: Cognitive Models & Mental Models
items.text: Cognitive Models & Mental Models The goals users want to achieve with the system The methods chosen to complete a particular task The basic physical or mental actions required for tasks The rules used to select among possible task methods

items.title: What is the Keystroke-Level Model (KLM) used for?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 3: Cognitive Models & Mental Models
items.text: Cognitive Models & Mental Models Measuring users' emotional reactions to an interface Estimating task duration from standard physical and mental actions Designing interactive prototypes with realistic visual details Organizing interview responses into common research themes

items.title: What design error occurs when a button is clicked but no loading spinner or success message appears?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 3: Cognitive Models & Mental Models
items.text: Cognitive Models & Mental Models Poor mapping, where controls do not match their functions Hidden feedback, where the system shows no clear response Poor visibility, where important functions are difficult to find Incorrect affordance, where controls suggest the wrong action

items.title: What is 'poor mapping' in software design?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 3: Cognitive Models & Mental Models
items.text: Cognitive Models & Mental Models Missing location data in a digital application Controls are arranged in ways that do not match their functions Text and images are not aligned along a visual grid System responses take longer than users expect

items.title: What is redesigning for alignment?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 3: Cognitive Models & Mental Models
items.text: Cognitive Models & Mental Models Changing visual details without considering user behavior Keeping unfamiliar control placements despite user confusion Adjusting the design to match users' natural expectations Replacing usability testing with automated code analysis

items.title: What is prototyping?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 4: Digital Prototyping & Interface Design
items.text: Digital Prototyping & Interface Design Writing the complete production code for the final system Building testable models before developing the actual system Preparing promotional materials for a finished application Collecting interview responses about users' experiences

items.title: What are low-fidelity prototypes?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 4: Digital Prototyping & Interface Design
items.text: Digital Prototyping & Interface Design Rough sketches showing basic screen structure and layout Interactive applications that closely resemble the final product Detailed digital models with realistic colors and typography Working systems containing finished backend functionality

items.title: What are tools like Figma and Adobe XD used for?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 4: Digital Prototyping & Interface Design
items.text: Digital Prototyping & Interface Design Developing backend code and software architecture Creating detailed, interactive interface prototypes Transcribing user interviews and coding research data Automatically testing every accessibility requirement

items.title: What is a reusable design part, such as a specific navigation bar, called?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 4: Digital Prototyping & Interface Design
items.text: Digital Prototyping & Interface Design A journey map describing the user's process A persona representing a group of users A component that can be reused across screens A wireframe showing a page's basic structure

items.title: What are the smooth animations that happen when navigating from one screen to the next called?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 4: Digital Prototyping & Interface Design
items.text: Digital Prototyping & Interface Design Microinteractions that give subtle responses to user actions Transitions that visually connect one screen to another Components that can be reused across different pages Wireframes that show the structure of an interface

items.title: What does responsive layout design ensure?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 4: Digital Prototyping & Interface Design
items.text: Digital Prototyping & Interface Design The interface adjusts to different screen sizes and layouts The system adapts its emotional response to each user The application's source code contains no programming errors Every button changes color whenever a user clicks it

items.title: Which approach forces a designer to prioritize only the most essential features first due to limited space?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 4: Digital Prototyping & Interface Design
items.text: Digital Prototyping & Interface Design Desktop-first design, which starts with large-screen layouts Mobile-first design, which starts with small-screen priorities High-fidelity design, which emphasizes realistic visual details Component-based design, which reuses interface elements

items.title: What is consistency in interface design?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 4: Digital Prototyping & Interface Design
items.text: Digital Prototyping & Interface Design Giving each page a completely different set of styles Maintaining familiar fonts, colors, and button styles across pages Arranging text and images without a structured grid Showing immediate visual responses to user actions

items.title: How does hierarchy guide the user's eye?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 4: Digital Prototyping & Interface Design
items.text: Digital Prototyping & Interface Design By hiding important features inside complicated menus By presenting every piece of text in the same size By using size, color, and spacing to show importance By providing spoken alerts for each interface element

items.title: What does checking for high color contrast in a prototype help improve?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 4: Digital Prototyping & Interface Design
items.text: Digital Prototyping & Interface Design The speed of animations between interface screens The size of files and their storage requirements Accessibility and readability for different users Backend processing and database performance

items.title: What is the purpose of user research in UCD?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 5: User Research, Journey Mapping & Ethics
items.text: User Research, Journey Mapping & Ethics To rely on assumptions about what users prefer To gather evidence about users' needs and behaviors To plan the software's internal programming structure To create the product's visual identity and branding

items.title: What type of research methods answer 'why' and 'how' a user behaves using detailed stories?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 5: User Research, Journey Mapping & Ethics
items.text: User Research, Journey Mapping & Ethics Quantitative methods that collect numerical data and statistics Qualitative methods that explore experiences and motivations Automated methods that scan systems for technical problems Algorithmic methods that calculate results through procedures

items.title: What is an interview guide?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 5: User Research, Journey Mapping & Ethics
items.text: User Research, Journey Mapping & Ethics A written transcript containing the complete interview conversation A prepared outline of open-ended research questions A formal agreement outlining the project's legal conditions A numerical survey used to measure user preferences

items.title: What is transcribing?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 5: User Research, Journey Mapping & Ethics
items.text: User Research, Journey Mapping & Ethics Highlighting repeated themes in collected research responses Creating fictional profiles of possible users Converting recorded spoken interviews into written text Writing source code to implement an application feature

items.title: How is a persona created accurately?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 5: User Research, Journey Mapping & Ethics
items.text: User Research, Journey Mapping & Ethics By guessing user characteristics from cultural stereotypes By grouping interview responses into shared behavior patterns By copying the design decisions of competing products By creating profiles without examining actual user research

items.title: What is the specific part of a system that a user interacts with on a journey map called?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 5: User Research, Journey Mapping & Ethics
items.text: User Research, Journey Mapping & Ethics An emotion describing how the user feels at a stage A pain point that makes a task difficult to complete A touchpoint where the user interacts with a system A wireframe outlining an interface's basic layout

items.title: By looking at emotional lows on a journey map, what can designers pinpoint?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 5: User Research, Journey Mapping & Ethics
items.text: User Research, Journey Mapping & Ethics Touchpoints where users interact with a system Personas representing different groups of users Pain points and opportunities for improvement Demographics describing users' personal backgrounds

items.title: What ethical requirement ensures users voluntarily agree to participate after knowing how their data will be used?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 5: User Research, Journey Mapping & Ethics
items.text: User Research, Journey Mapping & Ethics Respectful engagement that protects participants' dignity Data privacy that protects personal and sensitive information Informed consent based on clear study information User autonomy that supports independent personal choices

items.title: How must researchers protect user data identities in final reports?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 5: User Research, Journey Mapping & Ethics
items.text: User Research, Journey Mapping & Ethics By publishing participants' names with their responses By anonymizing identities in the final research report By sharing personal information with outside organizations By leaving identifying details visible in the collected data

items.title: What does respectful engagement in research involve?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 5: User Research, Journey Mapping & Ethics
items.text: User Research, Journey Mapping & Ethics Asking invasive questions regardless of participants' comfort Treating participants with dignity and avoiding potential harm Requiring every participant to finish the entire study Collecting only the information that supports a hypothesis

items.title: What is Accessibility?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 6: Accessibility and Inclusive Design
items.text: Accessibility and Inclusive Design Designing digital products mainly for the average user Ensuring digital products can be used by people with disabilities Providing applications for free download to all users Translating interface text into multiple languages

items.title: What is Inclusive Design?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 6: Accessibility and Inclusive Design
items.text: Accessibility and Inclusive Design Designing for the widest range of human diversity from the start Checking technical accessibility standards only after development Restricting product features to a limited group of users Designing exclusively for people with permanent disabilities

items.title: Using only the color red to convey an important error is a design barrier for which group?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 6: Accessibility and Inclusive Design
items.text: Accessibility and Inclusive Design Users who cannot rely on auditory alerts and sounds Users who have difficulty controlling physical movements Users with visual impairments, including color blindness Users who need support with memory, focus, or reading

items.title: What is a common design barrier for users with motor disabilities?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 6: Accessibility and Inclusive Design
items.text: Accessibility and Inclusive Design Missing captions for spoken and recorded video content Missing alternative text for images on a webpage Tiny clickable buttons placed too close together Complex wording that makes instructions hard to understand

items.title: What are the international standards for digital accessibility called?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 6: Accessibility and Inclusive Design
items.text: Accessibility and Inclusive Design HCI guidelines for designing human-computer interactions UCD stages for developing user-centered interfaces WCAG guidelines for accessible web content KLM methods for estimating the time needed for tasks

items.title: What does the 'O' in the POUR acronym stand for?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 6: Accessibility and Inclusive Design
items.text: Accessibility and Inclusive Design Organized, meaning content follows a consistent structure Operable, meaning users can navigate and use controls Objective, meaning information avoids personal opinions Optimized, meaning software performs tasks efficiently

items.title: What WCAG principle requires that content must not be invisible to all of a user's senses?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 6: Accessibility and Inclusive Design
items.text: Accessibility and Inclusive Design Perceivable, meaning users can sense the presented information Operable, meaning users can navigate available controls Understandable, meaning content and interactions are clear Robust, meaning content works with browsers and assistive tools

items.title: What level of WCAG compliance is the standard most websites are legally required to meet?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 6: Accessibility and Inclusive Design
items.text: Accessibility and Inclusive Design Level A, which provides the minimum accessibility features Level AA, which is the standard compliance target described Level AAA, which provides the highest compliance requirements Level B, which represents an additional WCAG compliance level

items.title: What assistive technology reads screen text out loud using a synthesized voice?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 6: Accessibility and Inclusive Design
items.text: Accessibility and Inclusive Design Adaptive switches that provide alternative physical controls Screen readers that convert on-screen information into speech Eye-tracking cameras that follow where a user is looking WAVE tools that highlight website accessibility issues

items.title: Why is manual testing essential alongside automated accessibility testing?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 6: Accessibility and Inclusive Design
items.text: Accessibility and Inclusive Design Automated tools cannot scan webpages quickly enough. Automated tools catch some issues but can miss context. Manual testing checks only the visual appearance of a website. Automated tools remove code that causes accessibility problems.

items.title: Why do HCI professionals have a strict ethical responsibility?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 7: Cultural Dimensions & Bias in Interfaces
items.text: Cultural Dimensions & Bias in Interfaces Technology affects people's daily lives, well-being, and autonomy. Hardware costs require designers to reduce development expenses. Business objectives must always take priority over user needs. Interface appearance is more important than users' safety.

items.title: What is an example of Persuasive Design and Dark Patterns?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 7: Cultural Dimensions & Bias in Interfaces
items.text: Cultural Dimensions & Bias in Interfaces Explaining the use of personal data before asking permission Making it intentionally difficult to cancel a subscription Translating interface content for a different target market Making controls larger to accommodate users with motor disabilities

items.title: What causes algorithmic bias in artificial intelligence systems?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 7: Cultural Dimensions & Bias in Interfaces
items.text: Cultural Dimensions & Bias in Interfaces Using research data that represents diverse groups of users Using flawed training data or reflecting programmers' unconscious bias Testing interactive prototypes with a range of participants Checking accessibility features with automated evaluation tools

items.title: Which ethical framework focuses entirely on the final outcome to achieve the greatest amount of good for the greatest number?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 7: Cultural Dimensions & Bias in Interfaces
items.text: Cultural Dimensions & Bias in Interfaces Deontology, which bases decisions on moral duties and rules Virtue Ethics, which emphasizes character and good intentions Utilitarianism, which seeks the greatest overall benefit User autonomy, which protects freedom of personal choice

items.title: What type of culture relies heavily on implicit understanding and visual cues rather than direct words?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 7: Cultural Dimensions & Bias in Interfaces
items.text: Cultural Dimensions & Bias in Interfaces Low-context culture, which favors direct and explicit information High-context culture, which relies on shared understanding and cues Individualistic culture, which emphasizes personal independence Collectivist culture, which emphasizes community and group harmony

items.title: What does the color red typically represent in many Asian cultures?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 7: Cultural Dimensions & Bias in Interfaces
items.text: Cultural Dimensions & Bias in Interfaces Danger and error in many common software interfaces Sadness and loss in various emotional design situations Luck, wealth, and success in many Asian cultural settings Confusion and frustration during difficult user interactions

items.title: What is stereotyping in personas?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 7: Cultural Dimensions & Bias in Interfaces
items.text: Cultural Dimensions & Bias in Interfaces Grouping real interview responses to identify behavior patterns Creating profiles from biased assumptions instead of research Testing prototypes with users who have different abilities Adapting interface content for specific cultural expectations

items.title: What type of design intentionally or accidentally creates barriers that shut out marginalized groups?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 7: Cultural Dimensions & Bias in Interfaces
items.text: Cultural Dimensions & Bias in Interfaces Inclusive design, which removes barriers for diverse users Exclusive design, which prevents some groups from accessing systems Iterative design, which improves solutions through repeated testing Responsive design, which adapts layouts to different screen sizes

items.title: What is Internationalization (i18n)?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 7: Cultural Dimensions & Bias in Interfaces
items.text: Cultural Dimensions & Bias in Interfaces Translating visible interface content into another language Preparing software architecture to support multiple languages and regions Replacing images to reflect a particular culture or market Changing currency and date formats for local users

items.title: What is Localization (l10n)?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 7: Cultural Dimensions & Bias in Interfaces
items.text: Cultural Dimensions & Bias in Interfaces Preparing software architecture for future language support Adapting interface text, formats, and images to a target market Establishing professional rules for ethical technology design Designing systems that accommodate users with disabilities

items.title: What negative emotions are triggered if an interface is slow and confusing?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 8: Designing for Emotion & User Engagement
items.text: Designing for Emotion & User Engagement Trust, satisfaction, and confidence during system use Delight, excitement, and enjoyment during everyday tasks Frustration, anxiety, and anger during difficult interactions Empathy, connection, and understanding toward other users

items.title: Which of Norman’s 3 levels of emotional design deals with immediate, subconscious reactions to aesthetics?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 8: Designing for Emotion & User Engagement
items.text: Designing for Emotion & User Engagement Visceral, which concerns appearance and first impressions Behavioral, which concerns usability, function, and performance Reflective, which concerns memory, meaning, and personal value Extrinsic, which concerns rewards and external consequences

items.title: What does intrinsic motivation mean in UX?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 8: Designing for Emotion & User Engagement
items.text: Designing for Emotion & User Engagement Using a system to earn a separate reward or badge Using a system because the activity itself is enjoyable Using an application mainly to avoid a negative outcome Logging in mainly to maintain a daily streak

items.title: According to Self-Determination Theory, giving users freedom of choice supports which psychological need?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 8: Designing for Emotion & User Engagement
items.text: Designing for Emotion & User Engagement Competence, which means feeling capable and successful Relatedness, which means feeling connected to other people Autonomy, which means controlling one's own actions and choices Extrinsic motivation, which means pursuing an outside reward

items.title: What is the practice of taking game-design elements and applying them to non-game systems called?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 8: Designing for Emotion & User Engagement
items.text: Designing for Emotion & User Engagement Prototyping, which tests early models of a digital system Gamification, which applies game elements to other activities Onboarding, which introduces users to an application's features Journey mapping, which tracks user actions and emotions

items.title: What specific tactic creates delight by doing something unexpected but positive, like a hidden mini-game?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 8: Designing for Emotion & User Engagement
items.text: Designing for Emotion & User Engagement Trust, which grows through security and predictable behavior Empathy, which responds to users' experiences and emotions Surprise, which creates positive reactions through unexpected moments Feedback, which confirms the outcome of a user action

items.title: What are tiny, single-purpose interactive moments that provide subtle feedback called?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 8: Designing for Emotion & User Engagement
items.text: Designing for Emotion & User Engagement Transitions, which animate movement between interface screens Components, which can be reused throughout an interface Microinteractions, which provide small responses to user actions Personas, which represent different types of system users

items.title: What is a 'flow state' in design?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 8: Designing for Emotion & User Engagement
items.text: Designing for Emotion & User Engagement A guided tutorial that explains system features one step at a time A state of deep focus and immersion without interruptions A journey map showing emotions throughout a user experience A technical process that transfers data between system parts

items.title: What is the crucial step-by-step process of guiding a brand-new user through an app's core features called?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 8: Designing for Emotion & User Engagement
items.text: Designing for Emotion & User Engagement Onboarding, which introduces users to the application's core features Retention, which measures users' continued use over time Evaluation, which checks a design against requirements Gamification, which adds points, levels, and other game elements

items.title: What visual survey uses pictures of a simple character showing different levels of emotion to measure UX?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 8: Designing for Emotion & User Engagement
items.text: Designing for Emotion & User Engagement Empathy maps, which organize what users say and feel Emotion cards, which help users describe their experiences AEQ questionnaires, which ask users to rate emotional responses SAM scale, which uses pictures to represent emotional states

items.title: How does AI shift HCI away from direct manipulation?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 9: Conversational AI & Voice Interfaces
items.text: Conversational AI & Voice Interfaces By requiring users to click every control manually By allowing users to state goals and delegate tasks to AI By making users write code for each requested operation By removing the need for natural language interaction

items.title: What allows a user to interact with a system using everyday human language rather than clicking menus?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 9: Conversational AI & Voice Interfaces
items.text: Conversational AI & Voice Interfaces Conversational Interface, which uses natural everyday language Tangible Interface, which uses real physical objects Graphic User Interface, which uses visual controls and menus Mixed Reality, which merges physical and digital environments

items.title: What AI technology helps computers understand the context and intent behind a user's words?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 9: Conversational AI & Voice Interfaces
items.text: Conversational AI & Voice Interfaces Object-Oriented Programming, which organizes software code Virtual Reality, which creates computer-generated environments Natural Language Processing, which analyzes human language Keystroke-Level Model, which estimates task completion time

items.title: What is a key design challenge specific to Voice User Interfaces (VUIs)?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 9: Conversational AI & Voice Interfaces
items.text: Conversational AI & Voice Interfaces They cannot operate with any spoken commands. They lack visual cues that reveal the available options. They can understand only direct commands written as code. They require a mouse to confirm every requested action.

items.title: How do designers typically prototype a conversation instead of drawing screens?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 9: Conversational AI & Voice Interfaces
items.text: Conversational AI & Voice Interfaces By constructing a physical model of the computer hardware By writing dialogue scripts and mapping conversation flowcharts By using accessibility scanners to examine interface layouts By preparing visual mockups for every possible screen

items.title: What is Wizard of Oz Testing in conversational interfaces?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 9: Conversational AI & Voice Interfaces
items.text: Conversational AI & Voice Interfaces Testing a fully functional AI that generates all replies itself Having a human provide replies that appear to come from AI Creating an immersive simulation for virtual reality users Using software to scan a webpage for accessibility errors

items.title: Why do evaluators test Error Recovery in voice interfaces?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 9: Conversational AI & Voice Interfaces
items.text: Conversational AI & Voice Interfaces Users may mumble or use slang, so the system must handle confusion. Voice systems must measure battery life during conversations. Spoken interfaces require the same visual color-contrast checks. Evaluators need to repair physical damage to audio hardware.

items.title: What does Testing Latency measure?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 9: Conversational AI & Voice Interfaces
items.text: Conversational AI & Voice Interfaces The volume of a user's voice during an interaction The accuracy of identifying the user's intended goal The delay between the user speaking and AI responding The number of words spoken throughout the conversation

items.title: What does Intent Recognition Testing measure?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 9: Conversational AI & Voice Interfaces
items.text: Conversational AI & Voice Interfaces The delay before the system begins to provide a response How accurately AI understands a goal despite different wording The user's emotional response to the interface appearance The display resolution available on the user's device

items.title: What must a VUI do to confirm actions since the user cannot 'see' the menu?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 9: Conversational AI & Voice Interfaces
items.text: Conversational AI & Voice Interfaces Print a paper receipt after processing every spoken command Change the screen color when the user finishes speaking Speak available options and provide clear audio feedback Require users to select visible buttons before each response

items.title: Which technology completely immerses the user in a 100% computer-generated environment, blocking out the physical world?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 10: Mixed Reality (AR/VR) & Tangible Interfaces
items.text: Mixed Reality (AR/VR) & Tangible Interfaces Augmented Reality, which overlays digital elements onto surroundings Virtual Reality, which immerses users in a generated environment Tangible Interface, which connects digital information to objects Ubiquitous Computing, which embeds technology into everyday spaces

items.title: Which technology overlays digital elements (like 3D graphics) onto the real physical world?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 10: Mixed Reality (AR/VR) & Tangible Interfaces
items.text: Mixed Reality (AR/VR) & Tangible Interfaces Virtual Reality, which blocks out the user's physical surroundings Augmented Reality, which adds digital elements to real surroundings Desktop UI, which presents controls through windows and menus Conversational AI, which responds through text or spoken language

items.title: What is Mixed Reality (MR)?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 10: Mixed Reality (AR/VR) & Tangible Interfaces
items.text: Mixed Reality (AR/VR) & Tangible Interfaces An interface that presents information only through written text A technology where physical and digital worlds interact in real time A virtual reality headset operating without an active display A mobile application that uses standard buttons and menus

items.title: What type of interface allows users to interact with digital information by manipulating real, physical objects?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 10: Mixed Reality (AR/VR) & Tangible Interfaces
items.text: Mixed Reality (AR/VR) & Tangible Interfaces Conversational Interface, which relies on natural language Graphic User Interface, which relies on visual controls Tangible User Interface, which uses physical objects as controls Voice User Interface, which relies on spoken interactions

items.title: How is VR used safely in education?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 10: Mixed Reality (AR/VR) & Tangible Interfaces
items.text: Mixed Reality (AR/VR) & Tangible Interfaces By completing written examinations on a flat display By simulating hazardous chemistry experiments without real danger By recording attendance through classroom information systems By preparing essays with a standard digital keyboard

items.title: What is Cybersickness (Motion Sickness) in VR?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 10: Mixed Reality (AR/VR) & Tangible Interfaces
items.text: Mixed Reality (AR/VR) & Tangible Interfaces A software virus that damages virtual reality applications Nausea caused by a mismatch between visual and body movement Eye fatigue resulting from bright colors on a headset display Arm discomfort resulting from repeated physical movements

items.title: What causes the physical fatigue known as 'Gorilla Arm'?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 10: Mixed Reality (AR/VR) & Tangible Interfaces
items.text: Mixed Reality (AR/VR) & Tangible Interfaces Wearing a headset that places weight on the user's head Holding raised arms to interact with virtual menus for long periods Moving around furniture while immersed in a digital environment Typing for long periods using a small physical keyboard

items.title: Which of the following is an environmental interference challenge for AR?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 10: Mixed Reality (AR/VR) & Tangible Interfaces
items.text: Mixed Reality (AR/VR) & Tangible Interfaces Users may become nauseated by visual movement in a headset. Poor lighting can prevent a camera from mapping a room accurately. Users may feel disconnected while interacting with digital content. Physical objects may not provide obvious interactive controls.

items.title: Why do evaluators use Dual-Video Observation for AR/VR?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 10: Mixed Reality (AR/VR) & Tangible Interfaces
items.text: Mixed Reality (AR/VR) & Tangible Interfaces To automatically locate programming errors during testing To record users' physical movements and their headset view To broadcast the testing session to a live online audience To calculate the delay between spoken input and audio response

items.title: What is a major physical safety challenge in VR?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 10: Mixed Reality (AR/VR) & Tangible Interfaces
items.text: Mixed Reality (AR/VR) & Tangible Interfaces A headset battery may become too hot during extended use. Users may hit walls or trip over objects they cannot see. Bright sunlight may reduce visibility on the display. Internet interruptions may prevent online content from loading.

items.title: What is the concept where computing is made to appear anytime and everywhere, fading into the background?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 11: Ubiquitous Computing & Smart Environments
items.text: Ubiquitous Computing & Smart Environments Mixed Reality, which combines physical and digital worlds Ubiquitous Computing, which embeds technology in everyday life Tangible Interface, which uses objects to manipulate digital content Graphic UI, which presents information through visible controls

items.title: What is a Smart Environment?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 11: Ubiquitous Computing & Smart Environments
items.text: Ubiquitous Computing & Smart Environments A space that monitors surroundings and responds to occupants' needs A classroom that provides fast internet access for students A mobile phone that contains many different applications A database server that stores information for other systems

items.title: What technology is actually used to build UbiComp by connecting physical devices to the internet?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 11: Ubiquitous Computing & Smart Environments
items.text: Ubiquitous Computing & Smart Environments Augmented Reality, which overlays content onto physical surroundings Natural Language Processing, which interprets human language Internet of Things, which connects physical devices to networks Adobe XD, which supports interactive interface prototyping

items.title: What is a key characteristic of UbiComp known as 'Invisibility' (Calm Computing)?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 11: Ubiquitous Computing & Smart Environments
items.text: Ubiquitous Computing & Smart Environments Devices use transparent materials to blend into their surroundings. Technology operates quietly without demanding constant attention. Software source code remains hidden from all system users. Devices operate without requiring electrical power or charging.

items.title: What does Context-Awareness allow a UbiComp system to do?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 11: Ubiquitous Computing & Smart Environments
items.text: Ubiquitous Computing & Smart Environments Print documents automatically whenever a device is connected Use time, location, and activity to anticipate users' needs Display information on a connected screen or monitor Create graphic layouts according to predefined design rules

items.title: What is a major privacy challenge in UbiComp?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 11: Ubiquitous Computing & Smart Environments
items.text: Ubiquitous Computing & Smart Environments Connected devices may gather too little environmental information. Constant monitoring can create risks of breaches and surveillance. Users may forget passwords for their connected devices. Small screens may make privacy notices harder to read.

items.title: What happens if the physical Hardware Layer of a smart environment loses power or breaks?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 11: Ubiquitous Computing & Smart Environments
items.text: Ubiquitous Computing & Smart Environments The environment automatically switches to solar power. Smart functions may stop when essential hardware fails. The software automatically repairs the damaged sensors. The environment switches its operation to virtual reality.

items.title: What software challenge makes it difficult for different brands (like Apple, Google, Philips) to communicate seamlessly in a smart home?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 11: Ubiquitous Computing & Smart Environments
items.text: Ubiquitous Computing & Smart Environments Algorithmic bias, which can produce unfair automated decisions Interoperability, which affects communication between different systems Latency, which creates delays in system responses Gamification, which adds game elements to everyday activities

items.title: How do designers map out when and where a user triggers a sensor before touching electronics?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 11: Ubiquitous Computing & Smart Environments
items.text: Ubiquitous Computing & Smart Environments By writing backend code that controls the hardware functions By using scenario mapping and storyboarding to plan interactions By running accessibility audits on the system's interface By building detailed interface prototypes in Figma

items.title: What affordable microcontrollers are usually used by developers to prototype the physical Hardware Layer?
items.meta: Study Cards · Lesson 11: Ubiquitous Computing & Smart Environments
items.text: Ubiquitous Computing & Smart Environments Supercomputers used to perform large-scale calculations High-end smartphones used for mobile applications Arduino or Raspberry Pi boards used for hardware prototypes Virtual reality headsets used for immersive digital experiences

items.title: Human-Computer Interaction (HCI)
items.meta: Glossary · see Topic 1: What is Human-Computer Interaction?
items.snippet: The study and design of how people interact with computers, so technology is useful, usable and safe.
items.text: The study and design of how people interact with computers, so technology is useful, usable and safe.

items.title: Usability
items.meta: Glossary · see Topic 4: The Usability Components
items.snippet: How easily and efficiently people can use a product to reach their goals, and how satisfied they are doing it.
items.text: How easily and efficiently people can use a product to reach their goals, and how satisfied they are doing it.

items.title: User Experience (UX)
items.meta: Glossary · see Topic 3: The Core Principles of HCI
items.snippet: The whole experience a person has with a product: how it works, how it feels and how it fits their needs.
items.text: The whole experience a person has with a product: how it works, how it feels and how it fits their needs.

items.title: User-Centered Design (UCD)
items.meta: Glossary · see Topic 11: What is User-Centered Design (UCD)?
items.snippet: A design process that keeps users' needs, goals and limits at the center of every stage, with repeated testing.
items.text: A design process that keeps users' needs, goals and limits at the center of every stage, with repeated testing.

items.title: Design Thinking
items.meta: Glossary · see Topic 8: What is Design Thinking?
items.snippet: A human-centered problem-solving approach: Empathize, Define, Ideate, Prototype and Test, repeated as needed.
items.text: A human-centered problem-solving approach: Empathize, Define, Ideate, Prototype and Test, repeated as needed.

items.title: Empathy Map
items.meta: Glossary · see Topic 17: Tools for Empathy & Design
items.snippet: A chart of what a user says, thinks, does and feels, used to build a shared understanding of them.
items.text: A chart of what a user says, thinks, does and feels, used to build a shared understanding of them.

items.title: Persona
items.meta: Glossary · see Topic 46: What are Personas?
items.snippet: A fictional but research-based user profile with goals, needs and frustrations that represents a user group.
items.text: A fictional but research-based user profile with goals, needs and frustrations that represents a user group.

items.title: Journey Map
items.meta: Glossary · see Topic 49: What is a Journey Map?
items.snippet: A visual timeline of the steps, touchpoints and emotions a user goes through to reach a goal.
items.text: A visual timeline of the steps, touchpoints and emotions a user goes through to reach a goal.

items.title: Pain Point
items.meta: Glossary · see Topic 50: Journey Mapping: Fixing User Frustrations
items.snippet: A moment in the user's journey where they feel frustrated, confused or blocked.
items.text: A moment in the user's journey where they feel frustrated, confused or blocked.

items.title: Mental Model
items.meta: Glossary · see Topic 18: What is Mental Models?
items.snippet: A user's own idea of how a system works, which shapes what they expect it to do.
items.text: A user's own idea of how a system works, which shapes what they expect it to do.

items.title: Cognitive Load
items.meta: Glossary · see Topic 92: The Four Key Visual Tools
items.snippet: The mental effort needed to use an interface. Good design keeps it low by reducing what users must remember.
items.text: The mental effort needed to use an interface. Good design keeps it low by reducing what users must remember.

items.title: Affordance
items.meta: Glossary · see Topic 20: Key Principles of Shaping Mental Models
items.snippet: A property of an object that suggests how it can be used, like a button that looks pressable.
items.text: A property of an object that suggests how it can be used, like a button that looks pressable.

items.title: Signifier
items.meta: Glossary · see Topic 20: Key Principles of Shaping Mental Models
items.snippet: A visible cue that shows where or how to act, such as a label, icon or arrow.
items.text: A visible cue that shows where or how to act, such as a label, icon or arrow.

items.title: Feedback
items.meta: Glossary · see Topic 3: The Core Principles of HCI
items.snippet: The system's response to an action, such as a spinner, sound or message, so users know what happened.
items.text: The system's response to an action, such as a spinner, sound or message, so users know what happened.

items.title: Mapping
items.meta: Glossary · see Topic 26: Design Implications: Errors and Alignment
items.snippet: The relationship between controls and their effects; natural mapping makes it obvious which control does what.
items.text: The relationship between controls and their effects; natural mapping makes it obvious which control does what.

items.title: Constraints
items.snippet: Limits that prevent wrong actions, like greying out a button until a form is complete.
items.text: Limits that prevent wrong actions, like greying out a button until a form is complete.

items.title: Consistency
items.meta: Glossary · see Topic 40: The Four Pillars of UI Design
items.snippet: Using the same patterns, words and styles throughout, so users can reuse what they already learned.
items.text: Using the same patterns, words and styles throughout, so users can reuse what they already learned.

items.title: Norman's Model of Interaction
items.meta: Glossary · see Topic 6: Types of Interaction Model
items.snippet: Don Norman's seven-stage action cycle, split into Execution (doing) and Evaluation (checking the result).
items.text: Don Norman's seven-stage action cycle, split into Execution (doing) and Evaluation (checking the result).

items.title: Gulf of Execution
items.meta: Glossary · see Topic 6: Types of Interaction Model
items.snippet: The gap between what a user wants to do and the actions the system allows.
items.text: The gap between what a user wants to do and the actions the system allows.

items.title: Gulf of Evaluation
items.meta: Glossary · see Topic 6: Types of Interaction Model
items.snippet: The gap between the system's state and the user's understanding of whether their action worked.
items.text: The gap between the system's state and the user's understanding of whether their action worked.

items.title: GOMS
items.meta: Glossary · see Topic 22: Components of GOMS Model
items.snippet: A cognitive model that breaks a task into Goals, Operators, Methods and Selection rules to predict user performance.
items.text: A cognitive model that breaks a task into Goals, Operators, Methods and Selection rules to predict user performance.

items.title: Keystroke-Level Model (KLM)
items.meta: Glossary · see Topic 21: The Cognitive Models in HCI
items.snippet: A GOMS variant that predicts task time by adding up standard times for keystrokes, pointing and thinking.
items.text: A GOMS variant that predicts task time by adding up standard times for keystrokes, pointing and thinking.

items.title: Fitts' Law
items.snippet: The time to reach a target depends on its distance and size: bigger and closer targets are faster to hit.
items.text: The time to reach a target depends on its distance and size: bigger and closer targets are faster to hit.

items.title: Hick's Law
items.snippet: The more choices people have, the longer it takes them to decide.
items.text: The more choices people have, the longer it takes them to decide.

items.title: Gestalt Principles
items.snippet: Rules for how people group what they see: proximity, similarity, closure, continuity and figure-ground.
items.text: Rules for how people group what they see: proximity, similarity, closure, continuity and figure-ground.

items.title: Nielsen's 10 Usability Heuristics
items.snippet: Jakob Nielsen's ten rules of thumb for usable interfaces, such as visibility of system status and error prevention.
items.text: Jakob Nielsen's ten rules of thumb for usable interfaces, such as visibility of system status and error prevention.

items.title: Heuristic Evaluation
items.snippet: An expert review that checks an interface against a set of usability heuristics.
items.text: An expert review that checks an interface against a set of usability heuristics.

items.title: Wireframe
items.meta: Glossary · see Topic 28: Fidelity Levels in Prototyping
items.snippet: A simple layout of a screen that shows structure and content placement without visual styling.
items.text: A simple layout of a screen that shows structure and content placement without visual styling.

items.title: Low-Fidelity Prototype
items.meta: Glossary · see Topic 28: Fidelity Levels in Prototyping
items.snippet: A rough, quick model (paper sketches or simple wireframes) used to test ideas early and cheaply.
items.text: A rough, quick model (paper sketches or simple wireframes) used to test ideas early and cheaply.

items.title: High-Fidelity Prototype
items.meta: Glossary · see Topic 28: Fidelity Levels in Prototyping
items.snippet: A detailed, interactive model that looks and behaves close to the final product.
items.text: A detailed, interactive model that looks and behaves close to the final product.

items.title: Usability Testing
items.meta: Glossary · see Topic 12: The 4 Stages of the User-Centered Design (UCD) Process
items.snippet: Watching real users try tasks with a product to find problems and improve the design.
items.text: Watching real users try tasks with a product to find problems and improve the design.

items.title: Think-Aloud Protocol
items.meta: Glossary · see Topic 124: Evaluation Methods for AR/VR
items.snippet: A testing method where users say what they are thinking while they use a product.
items.text: A testing method where users say what they are thinking while they use a product.

items.title: A/B Testing
items.snippet: Comparing two versions of a design with real users to see which one performs better.
items.text: Comparing two versions of a design with real users to see which one performs better.

items.title: Accessibility
items.meta: Glossary · see Topic 54: What is Accessibility?
items.snippet: Designing so people with disabilities can perceive, understand, navigate and use a product.
items.text: Designing so people with disabilities can perceive, understand, navigate and use a product.

items.title: WCAG (POUR)
items.meta: Glossary · see Topic 60: The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) Principles (POUR)
items.snippet: The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, built on four principles: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable and Robust.
items.text: The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, built on four principles: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable and Robust.

items.title: Assistive Technology
items.meta: Glossary · see Topic 63: What is Assistive Technologies?
items.snippet: Tools that help people with disabilities use computers, such as screen readers, magnifiers and switch controls.
items.text: Tools that help people with disabilities use computers, such as screen readers, magnifiers and switch controls.

items.title: Inclusive Design
items.meta: Glossary · see Topic 55: What is Inclusive Design?
items.snippet: Designing for the full range of human diversity, including ability, language, culture and age.
items.text: Designing for the full range of human diversity, including ability, language, culture and age.

items.title: Dark Patterns
items.meta: Glossary · see Topic 70: The Common Ethical Dilemmas
items.snippet: Deceptive design tricks that push users into actions they did not intend, like hidden costs or forced sign-ups.
items.text: Deceptive design tricks that push users into actions they did not intend, like hidden costs or forced sign-ups.

items.title: Hofstede's Cultural Dimensions
items.meta: Glossary · see Topic 74: Cultural Dimensions: Hofstede’s Framework
items.snippet: A framework that compares cultures on dimensions such as power distance and individualism, used in global design.
items.text: A framework that compares cultures on dimensions such as power distance and individualism, used in global design.

items.title: Emotional Design
items.meta: Glossary · see Topic 82: Norman’s 3 Levels of Emotional Design
items.snippet: Don Norman's idea that design affects people on three levels: visceral (looks), behavioral (use) and reflective (meaning).
items.text: Don Norman's idea that design affects people on three levels: visceral (looks), behavioral (use) and reflective (meaning).

items.title: Conversational User Interface
items.meta: Glossary · see Topic 102: What is a Conversational Interface?
items.snippet: An interface people use through natural language, such as a chatbot.
items.text: An interface people use through natural language, such as a chatbot.

items.title: Voice User Interface (VUI)
items.meta: Glossary · see Topic 104: What is a Voice User Interface (VUI)?
items.snippet: An interface controlled by speech, like a smart speaker assistant.
items.text: An interface controlled by speech, like a smart speaker assistant.

items.title: Augmented Reality (AR)
items.meta: Glossary · see Topic 111: The Differences between VR vs. AR vs. MR
items.snippet: Adds digital content on top of the real world, usually through a phone camera or glasses.
items.text: Adds digital content on top of the real world, usually through a phone camera or glasses.

items.title: Virtual Reality (VR)
items.meta: Glossary · see Topic 111: The Differences between VR vs. AR vs. MR
items.snippet: A fully digital, immersive environment experienced through a headset.
items.text: A fully digital, immersive environment experienced through a headset.

items.title: Tangible User Interface
items.meta: Glossary · see Topic 112: What is a Tangible User Interface (TUI)?
items.snippet: An interface where people control digital information by handling physical objects.
items.text: An interface where people control digital information by handling physical objects.

items.title: Ubiquitous Computing (UbiComp)
items.meta: Glossary · see Topic 125: What is UbiComp (Ubiquitous Computing)?
items.snippet: Computing built into everyday objects and spaces so it works in the background, anywhere.
items.text: Computing built into everyday objects and spaces so it works in the background, anywhere.

items.title: Context-Awareness
items.meta: Glossary · see Topic 134: Core Characteristics of UbiComp
items.snippet: A system's ability to sense its situation (location, time, activity) and adapt to it.
items.text: A system's ability to sense its situation (location, time, activity) and adapt to it.
